requirements: The analytical performance models for NVIDIA Blackwell (B200) and AMD CDNA3 (MI300A), their microbenchmark-derived parameters, and their validation on microbenchmarks, Rodinia 3.1, SPEChpc 2021 Tiny, and cross-platform ports to H200 and MI250X have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The evaluation hardware, drivers, and software stacks used for microbenchmarking, profiling, and validation on B200, MI300A, H200, and MI250X are available and configured.
Hardware evaluation platforms (Table VIII) required for microbenchmarking and validation are provisioned and identifiable to the pipeline.

Code has been implemented to detect and record access to an NVIDIA Blackwell B200 GPU as the primary NVIDIA evaluation platform (Table VIII), storing the SKU/board ID and reporting an error if the device is not visible via nvidia-smi.
Code has been implemented to detect and record access to an AMD Instinct MI300A APU (Table VIII) via rocminfo/rocm-smi and expose the socket/APU designation to the microbenchmark harness.
Code has been implemented to detect and record an NVIDIA H200 141 GB HBM3e GPU as the secondary NVIDIA platform used for the cross-platform Rodinia/SPEChpc port (Table VIII).
Code has been implemented to detect and record an AMD Instinct MI250X GPU as the secondary AMD platform for the CDNA2 port (Table VIII).
Driver, toolkit, and OS stacks reported in Section V-B/Table VIII are installed and version-checked by the environment setup scripts.

Environment setup code verifies that NVIDIA driver 550.163 and CUDA 12.4 are installed on the B200/H200 hosts (matching the versions reported in Table VIII) and fails loudly if a different version is detected.
Environment setup code verifies that ROCm 7.2.0 is installed on the MI300A host (matching Table VIII) and captures the reported version in the run metadata.
The OS versions in Table VIII are recorded: Linux 4.18.0-553.16.1.el8_10.x86_64 (MI300A host) and Linux 6.x (B200/H200 hosts), and are asserted before each validation run.
Profiling and optimized-library dependencies needed to produce the validation numbers are installed and callable from the benchmark scripts.
Nsight Compute and Nsight Systems are installed on the NVIDIA hosts, and the pipeline can invoke ncu/nsys to collect cuda_gpu_kern_sum kernel durations used as the NVIDIA ground truth (Section V-B).
ROCProfiler (rocprof) is installed on the MI300A host and the pipeline can invoke `rocprof --stats` to obtain HIP kernel durations used as the AMD ground truth (Section V-B).

Optimized vendor libraries required for the compute-bound microbenchmark kernels — cuBLAS/CUTLASS on NVIDIA and rocBLAS on AMD — are available on the PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH of the benchmark hosts (Section V-B).
The measurement protocol metadata specified in Table V is captured and enforced across every microbenchmark run.

Code has been implemented to record the Table V metadata bundle (GPU SKU/stepping, driver+firmware version, CUDA/ROCm toolkit version, power/clocks policy, microbenchmark binary list, validation app list) into a per-run metadata JSON alongside every timing file.

Code has been implemented to lock GPU clocks / enable persistence mode (nvidia-smi -pm 1 / rocm-smi --setperfdeterminism) or explicitly record the default policy, matching the platform lock-in requirement in Section V-B.

The microbenchmark harness runs each kernel 100 times after 10 warm-up iterations and reports the median execution time, exactly as specified in Section V-B, and asserts this in a unit test on a synthetic kernel.

Code has been implemented to enforce use of the same GPU stepping, driver stack, and power/clock policy across microbenchmark characterization runs and validation runs (platform lock-in per Section V-B); a mismatch between the recorded characterization metadata and the validation-run metadata raises an error.

Microbenchmarks for Blackwell B200 (TMEM read/write bandwidth, TMA copy latency, tcgen05.mma tensor core latency/throughput, mbarrier wait/commit latency) are implemented and reproduce the paper's measured parameter values reported in Table II and Table VII.
The Blackwell microbenchmark suite has a top-level structural scaffold: source layout, build system, and driver entry point that can enumerate and run all Blackwell microbenchmarks reproducibly.

Code has been implemented that organizes the Blackwell microbenchmarks under a dedicated directory (e.g. `microbench/blackwell/`) containing separate source files for TMEM bandwidth, TMA copy, mbarrier, and tcgen05.mma latency/throughput measurements.

Code has been implemented that provides a build script (Makefile or CMake) targeting SM_100 (Blackwell) with CUDA 12.4 and NVCC flags required to emit `tcgen05.mma`, `tcgen05.cp`, `cp.async.bulk`, and `mbarrier` PTX/SASS.

Code has been implemented that provides a driver script that runs every Blackwell microbenchmark with 10 warm-up iterations followed by 100 measured iterations and reports the median value for each metric, matching the paper's Section V-B measurement protocol.

Code has been implemented that writes measured Blackwell parameters (TMEM BW, TMA latency, tcgen05.mma latency, tensor throughput, mbarrier latencies) into a machine-readable parameter file (JSON/YAML) consumed by the Blackwell analytical model.

Code has been implemented that records measurement-protocol metadata (driver, CUDA version, GPU SKU, clock/persistence policy) alongside each Blackwell microbenchmark run, matching the metadata schema in Table V.
TMEM read/write bandwidth microbenchmark: tile-copy between TMEM and SMEM implemented and validated against the paper's measured bandwidths.
Code has been implemented that performs a TMEM↔SMEM tile copy kernel using `tcgen05.cp` (or equivalent TMEM load/store instructions) so that read and write bandwidth can be measured independently.

Code has been implemented that times the TMEM tile-copy over a sweep of tile sizes and converts (bytes transferred)/(elapsed seconds) into TB/s, reporting separate figures for the read (TMEM→SMEM) and write (SMEM→TMEM) directions.
The TMEM read-bandwidth microbenchmark reproduces the paper's measured value of ~16 TB/s (Table VII).
The TMEM write-bandwidth microbenchmark reproduces the paper's measured value of ~8 TB/s (Table VII).
Code has been implemented that verifies TMEM capacity per SM is 256 KB by allocating tensor-memory regions and confirming the reported per-SM allocation limit matches Table II.
TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) copy microbenchmark: measures TMA copy latency and effective bandwidth as a function of tile size and L2 residency.
Code has been implemented that issues an async TMA bulk copy (`cp.async.bulk.tensor` / `cp.async.bulk`) from global memory into shared memory to time a single TMA transaction.
Code has been implemented that measures TMA copy latency using GPU cycle counters (`%clock`/`%globaltimer` or SASS-level timestamps) between issue and mbarrier completion for a single small TMA copy.

Code has been implemented that sweeps TMA tile size and L2 residency (cache-hot vs cache-cold) and reports effective TMA bandwidth (bytes/latency) as a function of both, matching the Section V-A protocol.
The TMA copy-latency microbenchmark reproduces the paper's measured L_TMA of ~420 cycles (Table VII).
The HBM peak-bandwidth microbenchmark (used as the streaming reference for TMA bandwidth) reproduces the paper's measured value of ~8.0 TB/s on B200 (Table II).
mbarrier synchronization microbenchmark: measures the barrier wait latency L_mbar and commit latency L_commit used by the Blackwell model's T_sync term.
Code has been implemented that uses `mbarrier.init`, `mbarrier.arrive`, and `mbarrier.try_wait` to construct a single-CTA barrier round-trip whose latency can be timed.

Code has been implemented that separately isolates commit latency (`mbarrier.arrive`/tcgen05.commit) from wait latency (`mbarrier.try_wait`) by inserting cycle counters immediately before and after each phase.
The mbarrier wait-latency microbenchmark reproduces the paper's measured L_mbar of 40–50 cycles (Table VII).
The mbarrier commit-latency microbenchmark reproduces the paper's measured L_commit in the 40–50 cycle range (Table VII).
tcgen05.mma tensor-core microbenchmark: measures 5th-generation tensor-core instruction latency and throughput across supported precisions.

Code has been implemented that issues single `tcgen05.mma` instructions with operands staged in TMEM/SMEM and measures issue-to-complete latency in GPU cycles for the FP64, FP16, FP8, FP6, and FP4 precisions.
Code has been implemented that saturates the tensor-core pipeline with back-to-back `tcgen05.mma` issues to measure achieved throughput per SM in TFLOPS, sweeping across all supported precisions.
Code has been implemented that also exercises the 2-SM cooperative UMMA mode (S_mode = 2) so that per-CTA tensor throughput accounting used by the Blackwell model can be measured directly.
The tcgen05.mma per-instruction latency microbenchmark reproduces the paper's reported range of 11–14 cycles across FP64→FP4 precisions (Table VII).
The per-SM tensor throughput sweep reproduces the paper's measured range of 44.8–7702 TFLOPS across supported precisions (Table VII, R_SM^TC).
The FP16 tensor-core throughput measurement reproduces the paper's reported peak of ~2,250 TFLOPS on B200 (Table II).
The FP8 tensor-core throughput measurement reproduces the paper's reported peak of ~4,500 TFLOPS on B200 (Table II).
Blackwell hardware-parameter probes populate the remaining Table II entries directly from device properties or targeted microbenchmarks.
Code has been implemented that queries or measures the SM count on B200 and records 176 SMs (Table II).
Code has been implemented that records the Blackwell warp size as 32 threads (Table II).
A microbenchmark measures maximum resident warps per SM on B200 and reproduces the paper's value of 64 (Table II).
Code has been implemented that records the HBM3e capacity on B200 as 192 GB (Table II).
Code has been implemented that records the aggregate L2 cache size on B200 as 64 MB (Table II).
Code has been implemented that records the TMEM size per SM as 256 KB (Table II), consistent with the TMEM bandwidth microbenchmark's allocation ceiling.
Aggregation and export of Blackwell microbenchmark results into a form usable by the analytical model and downstream reports.

Code has been implemented that consolidates all Blackwell measurements into a single Table VII-style artifact keyed by parameter name (TMEM BW, L_TMA, tcgen05.mma latency, R_SM^TC, L_mbar, L_commit) with numeric values and units.

Code has been implemented that separates 'peak' (datasheet) from 'sustained' (microbenchmark) values for HBM bandwidth and tensor throughput in the exported Blackwell parameter file, matching the paper's Section V-A distinction.

Code has been implemented that reports median, IQR, and per-kernel error dispersion for every Blackwell microbenchmark so that the paper's claim of per-kernel IQR below 2% on B200 can be verified from the run output.

Microbenchmarks for MI300A (L1/L2/Infinity Cache/HBM bandwidth and latency, MFMA throughput/utilization vs tile size, LLC hit rate hLLC(W) sweep, interference and multi-GPU τ measurements) are implemented and reproduce the paper's parameter values.
The MI300A cache hierarchy bandwidth microbenchmark suite (HBM, Infinity Cache, L1/L2) is implemented and produces the reported sustained bandwidth values.

Code has been implemented for an HBM streaming bandwidth microbenchmark on MI300A (e.g., large-array HIP copy/triad kernel) that reports sustained GB/s and is exposed as an executable/entry point in the microbenchmark suite.

The HBM bandwidth microbenchmark sweeps working sets larger than the 256 MB Infinity Cache to guarantee HBM-resident behavior and emits a per-run bandwidth measurement in TB/s with median-of-repeats aggregation matching the paper's 100 runs / 10 warm-ups protocol.
The measured MI300A HBM peak bandwidth reported by the microbenchmark matches the paper's value of 5.3 TB/s (Table II / Table VII) within tolerance.

Code has been implemented for an Infinity Cache (LLC) bandwidth microbenchmark that pins the working set below the 205 MB fully-resident boundary and reports sustained bandwidth achievable when data hits in the 256 MB Infinity Cache.
The Infinity Cache bandwidth microbenchmark verifies cache residency (e.g., via ROCProfiler hit counters or the hLLC(W) model) so that reported bandwidth reflects LLC hits, not HBM traffic.
The measured MI300A Infinity Cache bandwidth reported by the microbenchmark matches the paper's value of 17.2 TB/s (Table VII) within tolerance.

Code has been implemented for L1 and L2 bandwidth microbenchmarks (e.g., small tile copies resident in L1/L2) that emit per-level bandwidth numbers used to parameterize BW_L1 and BW_L2 in the analytical model.
The MI300A cache/HBM latency microbenchmark (pointer-chasing per Mei & Chu / [27]) is implemented and reproduces the reported per-level cycle latencies used to parameterize the MI300A model.

Code has been implemented for a pointer-chasing latency microbenchmark on MI300A that varies stride/working-set size to isolate L1, L2, LLC (Infinity Cache), and HBM latencies and reports latency in cycles.

The pointer-chasing benchmark uses a chain layout (dependent loads, unfixed pattern) that defeats hardware prefetching and produces a monotonically increasing latency curve as working-set size crosses each cache level boundary.
The measured L1 latency on MI300A matches the paper's value of ~5 cycles (Table VII) within tolerance.
The measured L2 latency on MI300A matches the paper's value of ~50 cycles (Table VII) within tolerance.
The measured Infinity Cache (LLC) latency on MI300A matches the paper's value of ~150 cycles (Table VII) within tolerance.
The measured HBM latency on MI300A matches the paper's value of ~400 cycles (Table VII) within tolerance.
The MI300A MFMA microbenchmarks (peak throughput per precision and utilization vs tile size) are implemented and reproduce the reported FP64/FP8 peaks and tile-size ordering.
Code has been implemented for an MFMA peak throughput microbenchmark on MI300A that issues back-to-back MFMA instructions for at least FP64 and FP8 precisions and reports achieved TFLOPS.

The MFMA peak throughput benchmark sustains dependence-free MFMA issue (accumulator-only dependencies, sufficient warp occupancy) so that the reported number reflects instruction throughput rather than memory or register-file stalls.
The measured FP64 MFMA peak throughput on MI300A matches the paper's value of 61.3 TFLOPS (Table II) within tolerance.
The measured FP8 MFMA peak throughput on MI300A matches the paper's value of 1,307 TFLOPS (Table II) within tolerance.
Code has been implemented for an MFMA utilization-vs-tile-size sweep on MI300A over the tile sizes referenced in the paper (8, 16, 32, 64) and reports per-tile achieved throughput / utilization.

The MFMA tile-sweep output preserves the paper's qualitative ordering (16x16 tiles measured faster than 8x8 tiles for the occupancy/tile GEMM case), matching the ordering used by the adaptive tile-selection model.
The MI300A Infinity Cache hit-rate sweep hLLC(W) is implemented and reproduces the three-regime piecewise model in Table III (fully-resident, transition, streaming).
Code has been implemented for a working-set sweep microbenchmark that varies W across the boundaries in Table III (below 205 MB, 205-256 MB, above 256 MB) and reports measured LLC hit rate per point.

The piecewise hLLC(W) function from Table III (1.0 for W<205 MB; linear transition on 205<=W<=256; (256/W)^beta streaming for W>256 MB) is implemented as a callable used by the analytical model, with alpha and beta parameters loaded from calibration data rather than hard-coded.
A calibration routine fits alpha and beta of hLLC(W) from the microbenchmark sweep by nonlinear regression against measured hit-rate points in the transition and streaming regimes.
The measured hLLC(W) sweep reproduces the fully-cache-resident regime with hLLC = 1.0 for all working sets W < 205 MB (Table III) within tolerance.
The measured hLLC(W) sweep reproduces the transition boundary at the 256 MB Infinity Cache capacity (Table III) - hit rate drops sharply as W crosses 256 MB, matching the paper's cache size.
The effective bandwidth blend BW_effective = hLLC*BW_LLC + (1-hLLC)*BW_HBM is implemented using the sweep-derived hLLC(W) and the microbenchmark-measured BW_LLC (17.2 TB/s) and BW_HBM (5.3 TB/s).
MI300A interference and multi-GPU microbenchmarks are implemented and produce the tau_interf and tau_interf_gpu values used by the analytical model.

Code has been implemented for a concurrent-stream interference microbenchmark on MI300A (1-stream vs 2-stream / 1-kernel vs N-kernel comparison on separate HIP streams) that isolates the per-additional-concurrent-kernel overhead.

The interference microbenchmark reports tau_interf in seconds (or microseconds) by fitting a linear model T_multi = T_base + (N_concurrent - 1) * tau_interf against measured multi-stream execution times.
The tuned MI300A multi-kernel interference overhead tau_interf produced by the microbenchmark matches the paper's value of 50 microseconds (Table VII) within tolerance.
Code has been implemented for a multi-GPU interference microbenchmark on MI300A (1-device vs 2-device execution of the same kernel) that isolates the per-additional-device overhead tau_interf_gpu.
The multi-GPU benchmark fits tau_interf_gpu via T_multi_gpu = T_base + (N_devices - 1) * tau_interf_gpu and writes the fitted value into the MI300A parameter file used by the analytical model.
Code has been implemented for a fusion microbenchmark (unfused GEMM+bias vs fused GEMM+bias) that produces the tau_fusion overhead used by the kernel-fusion path of the MI300A model.
MI300A occupancy, NUMA (cross-XCD), and resource-limit microbenchmarks are implemented and reproduce the reported architectural constants used by the wavefront-centric model.
Code has been implemented for a cross-XCD NUMA latency microbenchmark that issues loads targeting memory homed on a remote XCD and reports the additional latency vs a local-XCD access.
The measured cross-XCD NUMA-like access penalty on MI300A falls in the paper's reported 50-100 ns range (Section III).
Code has been implemented for an occupancy microbenchmark that sweeps launched wavefronts per CU and confirms the max-resident-wavefronts constant used by the model (32 per CU, Table II).

The MI300A parameter file consumed by the analytical model is populated from microbenchmark outputs and includes the datasheet-derived constants (304 CUs = 38 per XCD x 8 XCDs, 64-thread wavefront, 64 KB LDS per CU, 128 GB HBM, 256 MB LLC) from Table II.
The MI300A microbenchmark suite has a shared measurement protocol and driver harness matching the paper's methodology (100 runs, 10 warm-ups, median reporting, ROCProfiler-based verification).
A shared harness executes each MI300A microbenchmark for 10 warm-up iterations followed by 100 timed iterations and reports the median execution time, matching Section V-B.
The harness records platform lock-in metadata per Table V (ROCm version, driver, clock policy, microbenchmark binary/flags) alongside each measurement output so runs are reproducible.
Microbenchmark timings are cross-checked against ROCProfiler / rocprof --stats HIP kernel durations to align with the paper's 'measured time' definition on AMD platforms (Section V-B).

The suite emits a single machine-readable MI300A parameter file (JSON/YAML/etc.) aggregating BW_HBM, BW_LLC, per-level latencies, MFMA peaks, hLLC(W) coefficients, tau_interf, tau_interf_gpu, and tau_fusion in a schema consumed by the MI300A analytical model.

The Blackwell analytical model is implemented, including TMEM/tensor core compute (Eq. 3), TMA memory time (Eq. 4), decompression, sync/barriers, 2-SM cooperative (UMMA) execution, overlap α, writeback, TMEM amortized management, and per-step/full-kernel time composition.
Tensor core compute and TMEM residency modeling (Eq. 3): per-K-step TMEM time and per-CTA compute time expressions including 2-SM mode factor and TMEM capacity constraints.

Code has been implemented that defines a Blackwell tensor-core / TMEM compute submodule exposing a callable that returns per-CTA compute time given tile dimensions (bM, bN, bK), tensor throughput per SM, and the TMEM strategy.

Code has been implemented that computes per-K-step TMEM time as a function of TMEM read/write bandwidth, tile bytes moved between TMEM and SMEM, and the number of accumulator accesses per K-step (Eq. 3, K-step term).

Code has been implemented that computes per-CTA compute time from tensor-core throughput per SM RT_C[SM] and the number of tensor-core operations per CTA, dividing by the 2-SM cooperation factor S_mode when active.
Code has been implemented that flags or penalizes configurations whose per-SM TMEM footprint exceeds 256 KB, reflecting the spill-and-efficiency-loss behavior described in Section IV-A1.

Code has been implemented that supports TMEM strategy A (accumulators in TMEM, inputs in SMEM) and strategy B (A and accumulators in TMEM via tcgen08.cp) with distinct TMEM traffic accounting for each.
The implementation uses TMEM read/write bandwidths of 16 TB/s and 8 TB/s respectively as the default parameter values for the Blackwell B200 tensor-core/TMEM compute term (Table VII).
The tcgen05.mma per-instruction latency parameter used by the Blackwell compute term falls within the reported 11–14 cycle range across FP64 through FP4 precisions (Table VII).

The per-SM tensor throughput parameter RT_C[SM] used by the Blackwell compute term spans the 44.8 TFLOPS (FP64) to 7702 TFLOPS (lowest precision) range reported in Table VII across supported precisions.
TMA memory time modeling (Eq. 4) including multicast, per-CTA byte accounting, and A/B tile overlap handling.
Code has been implemented that defines a TMA memory-time submodule returning per-CTA TMA time from tile bytes, TMA latency L_TMA, and TMA bandwidth B_TMA.
Code has been implemented that reduces per-CTA bytes for TMA multicast as bytes_per_CTA = bytes(T)/P, where P is the number of participants sharing a tile.
Code has been implemented that allows the effective TMA bandwidth B_TMA to be adjusted based on an L2 hit-rate input, reflecting Section IV-A2's note that L2 residency strongly affects B_TMA.
Code has been implemented that composes A-tile and B-tile TMA times using either sum or max depending on an overlap flag, supporting distinct participant counts P_A and P_B on the two operands.
The TMA latency parameter L_TMA used by the memory-time term defaults to 420 cycles on B200, matching the microbenchmark value reported in Table VII.
The Blackwell parameter file used to instantiate the TMA and HBM terms uses HBM peak bandwidth 8.0 TB/s and HBM capacity 192 GB for B200 (Table II).
Decompression engine modeling including link-vs-engine load time, compression ratio / efficiency scaling, sub-byte unpacking cost, and overlap via α.
Code has been implemented that exposes a decompression submodule computing T_DE_load = max(D_compressed / BW_link, D_compressed / R_DE) for the link-vs-engine path.
Code has been implemented that incorporates a compression ratio CR and decompression efficiency η_DE into the effective decompression throughput used by the model.
Code has been implemented that computes sub-byte unpacking cost as T_decomp = bytes_comp / R_decomp + L_decomp_setup, exposing R_decomp and L_decomp_setup as parameters.
Code has been implemented that allows the decompression stage to overlap with compute and TMA via the same overlap factor α used elsewhere in the Blackwell model.
The decompression submodule advertises support for LZ4, Snappy, and Deflate formats consistent with the Blackwell decompression-engine description in Section III.
Sync and barrier modeling for Blackwell K-step pipelines.
Code has been implemented that computes T_sync per K-step as N_bar × L_mbar, exposing both N_bar and L_mbar as parameters.
The default N_bar per K-step used by the model falls in the 1–2 range described in Section IV-A3.
The default mbarrier latency L_mbar used by the model matches the 40–50 cycle range reported in Table VII for the Blackwell barrier microbenchmark.
The commit latency L_commit used by the 2-SM sync accounting matches the 40–50 cycle range reported in Table VII for the Blackwell barrier microbenchmark.
2-SM cooperative (UMMA) execution modeling: DSMEM traffic sharing, compute speedup, sync cost, and per-CTA time adjustments.
Code has been implemented that models CTA-pair traffic on adjacent SMs sharing B via DSMEM as D_2-CTA = 2*M_A + M_B instead of 2*(M_A + M_B).
Code has been implemented that computes 2-SM memory time as T_memory_2-CTA = (2*M_A + M_B) / BW_shared using the DSMEM shared-memory bandwidth parameter.
Code has been implemented that adds a 2-SM sync cost equal to K_tiles × L_commit to the 2-SM execution-time composition.
Code has been implemented that divides the single-SM compute time by a measured 2-SM speedup factor S_2SM when the 2-SM cooperative path is selected.
The 2-SM DSMEM sharing achieves the reported traffic reduction of approximately 1.33× for square tiles relative to independent-CTA traffic (Section IV-A4).
The predicted 2-SM cooperative speedup on the validation kernel is 1.30× compared with the measured value of 1.28×, reproducing the within-2% agreement reported in Section V.
Code has been implemented that exposes an S_mode / 2-SM toggle so that the tensor-core compute expression (Eq. 3) is divided by S_mode when 2-SM cooperation is enabled and by 1 otherwise.
Overlap factor α modeling for the Blackwell critical-path stage composition.
Code has been implemented that combines compute and I/O stages using an overlap factor α ∈ [0, 1] so that a fraction α of I/O is hidden behind compute (Section IV-A5).
The default α range used by the Blackwell model is 0.85–0.95, corresponding to double- to triple-buffering pipeline depth (Section IV-A3).
Code has been implemented that permits a sensitivity sweep over α (e.g., α ∈ {0.85, 0.90, 0.95}) and returns the resulting change in predicted per-step time.
Code has been implemented that documents the α parameter and its default and range so that model users can adjust it per workload without editing formula code.
Writeback and TMA-store modeling for output C tiles.
Code has been implemented that computes a global-memory writeback time T_store = bytes(C_tile) / B_gmem + L_store_setup for the non-TMA path.
Code has been implemented that alternatively computes a TMA-store writeback time L_TMA_store + bytes(C_tile) / B_TMA when TMA is used for stores.
Code has been implemented that allows writeback to be marked as overlapped and therefore excluded from the critical path when the kernel is persistent, matching the note in Section IV-A5.
The full-kernel composition adds T_writeback as a term in the Blackwell total-time expression T_Blackwell = T_launch + K_tiles × max(T_compute_TC, T_io_eff) + T_sync + T_writeback (Section IV-C).
TMEM amortized management cost modeling.
Code has been implemented that computes the amortized TMEM management overhead T_TMEM_mgmt_amortized = (L_alloc + L_dealloc) / K_tiles.
Code has been implemented that folds the amortized TMEM management term into the O_misc contribution of the per-step time composition.
Code has been implemented that exposes L_alloc and L_dealloc as separately configurable microbenchmark-derived latencies.
Per-step and full-kernel time composition, launch overhead, and pipeline bubble handling.
Code has been implemented that computes the steady-state pipelined per-step time T_step_pipelined = max(T_tma, T_decomp, T_compute, T_sync) + ε.
Code has been implemented that assembles the full per-step time by adding an O_misc contribution covering TMEM management and pipeline bubbles.
Code has been implemented that computes total kernel time as T_kernel = T_launch + K_tiles × T_step + T_writeback, matching the summary in Section IV-C.
Code has been implemented that exposes T_launch as a first-principles kernel-launch overhead parameter that can be sourced from a microbenchmark rather than hard-coded.
The Blackwell full-kernel composition treats T_compute_TC and T_io_eff as a max() at each of K_tiles iterations, matching the T_Blackwell expression in the Unified Summary (Section IV-C).
On the GEMM validation case with M=N=K=16384 and tile 128×128×32 on B200, the model predicts 4.17 ms compared with a measured 4.10 ms, reproducing the reported 1.8% error (Section IV-D).
The Blackwell model on the memory-bound microbenchmark subset (vector add/copy/transpose/reduction) achieves the reported 8.4% MAE.
The Blackwell model on the compute-bound microbenchmark subset (FP16/FP8/LLM GEMM via cuBLAS) achieves the reported 5.4% MAE.
The Blackwell model on the balanced microbenchmark subset (FFT, SpMV, GEMV) achieves the reported 7.9% MAE.
The Blackwell model on the SpMV kernel at 0.1% density shows the reported 13.6% error, attributable to unmodeled atomics and load imbalance.
When TMEM bandwidth is tuned to 24–26 TB/s (versus the conservative 22 TB/s default), the Blackwell compute-bound GEMM error reduces to the reported 2–3% range.
The vector-op memory-bound predictions on B200 exhibit a launch-overhead contribution consistent with the reported 5–12 µs range described in Section V-B.
Concurrent-stream and multi-GPU interference term extensions.
Code has been implemented that adds (N_c - 1) × τ_c to single-stream Blackwell time when N_c concurrent streams are specified.
Code has been implemented that adds (N_d - 1) × τ_g to single-GPU Blackwell time when N_d GPUs are specified.
Code has been implemented that treats both τ_c and τ_g as microbenchmark-fitted parameters rather than hard-coded values, mirroring the MI300A interference terms described in Section IV-A6.
Model workflow entrypoint: workload characterization, parameter selection, and per-workload prediction for the Blackwell path.
Code has been implemented that accepts workload inputs bM, bN, bK, K_tiles, bytes-per-CTA, TMA participants P, and overlap α as documented required inputs for the Blackwell path (Section IV-G).

Code has been implemented that loads Blackwell hardware parameters (SMs, warp size, HBM BW/capacity, L2 size, TMEM size, tensor peaks) from a parameter file so H200 or future GPUs can be substituted without formula changes (Table II).

Code has been implemented that provides a callable end-to-end prediction function taking (workload, parameters) and returning predicted kernel time by chaining T_launch, tile loop of max(compute, io), T_sync, and T_writeback (Section IV-D workflow).

The MI300A wavefront-centric analytical model is implemented, including cache-hierarchy effective memory time (Eq. 10), the hLLC(W) piecewise function (Table III), MFMA compute (Eq. 11), VGPR-limited occupancy, overlap η (Eq. 9), per-step and per-kernel time (Eq. 13), optional MWP/CWP limits, multi-kernel/multi-GPU interference terms, host-device transfer/sync, adaptive tile selection, and kernel fusion, with hardware parameters (304 CUs, 64-thread wavefronts, 32 resident wavefronts max, 256 MB Infinity Cache, 128 GB HBM) sourced from Table II and calibrated coefficients from Table VII.
The cache-hierarchy effective memory time (Eq. 10) and effective bandwidth formulation for MI300A are implemented, blending L1/L2/Infinity-Cache/HBM traffic weighted by measured hit rates.

Code has been implemented for the MI300A effective memory time (Eq. 10) as a function of per-level bytes, hit rates hL1, hL2, hLLC, and per-level bandwidths BW_L1, BW_L2, BW_LLC, BW_HBM, returning a scalar time in seconds.

The effective memory time function has been unit-tested: when hL1=hL2=0 and hLLC=1 with all traffic served from Infinity Cache, the returned time equals bytes / BW_LLC (within floating-point tolerance).
Code has been implemented for the effective bandwidth BW_effective = hLLC · BW_LLC + (1 − hLLC) · BW_HBM as a helper used by the memory-time and per-step formulas.
